data.title: 'Appetite for change': Van Hollen claims momentum in battle for Senate majority leader
data.description:
Congress

Sen. Chris Van Hollen says ‘momentum is in our direction’ in battle for majority leader

The Maryland senator also said he will not run for president in 2028, even if he loses the leadership bid.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Chris Van Hollen says ‘momentum’ is in his direction for Senate Democratic leader: Full interview
10:45
Get more newson
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 22, 2026, 10:51 AM EST
By Megan Brand

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that “momentum is in our direction” in his bid for Senate majority leader.

Asked directly how much support he had within the Democratic caucus, Van Hollen said the number is “north of 15” although it’s short of the 28 votes needed to win the leadership race against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.

Democratic senators and senators-elect will hold a vote in December to determine the next majority leader, a dominant role in shaping the party’s agenda and its response to the Trump administration.

Van Hollen’s allies have sought to frame him as a leader who can push for change, while Schumer’s allies have argued that his leadership helped usher in historic Democratic wins across the country.

Asked whether he believes he can secure enough votes, Van Hollen said yes.

“Yes, because if you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change,” he said in the Sunday interview. “They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate.”

Van Hollen also said he believes the Democratic Party is “on probation” and needs to earn Americans’ trust.

“You don’t earn people’s trust by going back to business as usual,” he said.

Van Hollen said he personally believes that the filibuster, which requires that most bills in the Senate need at least 60 votes to pass, “is an anti-democratic provision.”

“But I also understand that the job of the majority leader is to work with the caucus,” he continued.

“So we should set sort of standards and criteria for at what level of obstruction by Republicans — to root out political corruption, to move forward on voting rights — at what level will we consider alternatives?” he said, listing two major policy fights for which Democrats could potentially change the rules.

One possibility, he said, is requiring a talking filibuster so that Republicans would have to show their opposition to popular proposals on the Senate floor.

Van Hollen, who has been floated as a potential presidential candidate, also confirmed on “Meet the Press” that he will not run for president, even if he loses the leadership race. Van Hollen initially said he was “kicking the tires” on a presidential run, but after jumping in the Senate leadership race, he said he was not pursuing a presidential run anymore.

“After I saw the scope of this victory, this call from the American people, my view is now we have to deliver, we have to earn people’s trust, and that would be my focus entirely,” he said. “So no, I’m not running for president in 2028.”

data.title: Bay Area residents urged to avoid Thanksgiving travel as extreme flooding looms
data.description:
Bay Area airports, coast under extreme flood threat; residents told to avoid travel

Rong-Gong Lin II
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 5:10 PM UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The California coast could see all-time-high sea levels this week, with officials warning of the potential for major seawater flooding of coastal neighborhoods.

The San Francisco Bay Area faces an added threat because a strong storm will strike the region just as the highest tides so far this year arrive. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel early this week, with the city still reeling from exceptional flooding from last week's powerful rainstorm.

Problems are also likely on the Southern California coast, where sea levels could be even higher than when records were shattered Oct. 27, flooding homes and businesses in places such as Huntington Beach, Newport Beach, Long Beach, Redondo Beach and San Diego.

Advertisement

The dangerous weather is being fueled by El Niño, hot ocean temperatures and unusually powerful king tides that are among the highest in two decades. Unlike Southern California, Northern California will also see a moderate-to-heavy rainstorm starting Tuesday, expected to whip up larger breaking waves and add to the potential for flooding.

Even San Francisco International Airport and Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport are at risk of flooding, according to meteorologist Anamaria Navarrete of the National Weather Service's Monterey office, which warned of "extreme coastal flooding" on the San Francisco Bay shoreline.

"San Francisco could face a combination of exceptionally high tides, heavy rain and strong winds over the coming days," the mayor said in a video posted on social media. "And our waterfront is expecting king tides, which are anticipated to bring the highest tide levels in San Francisco's history.

"This is a warning that I want everybody to take seriously. We want you to avoid unnecessary travel, especially around these peak tide periods that are coming," Lurie said.

The San Francisco Department of Emergency Management suggested avoiding unnecessary travel starting Monday afternoon through Wednesday; Marin County officials urged the same between 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day, especially in flood-prone areas.

Crews were rushing to install emergency flood barriers along the bay shoreline, including at the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge toll plaza, where a "Tiger Dam" was installed. State transportation officials ordered the shutdown of the only vehicular route out of western Alameda to Oakland — the Posey Tube tunnel — starting Sunday night. And Marin County said people on the entire Tiburon Peninsula should consider leaving low-lying areas before the daily highest tide, starting Sunday through Black Friday, due to the flood risk.

Set during the most powerful El Niño on record — and during a confluence of extremely high tides and a big storm — the all-time maximum sea level at the San Francisco tidal gauge at Crissy Field was set on Jan. 27, 1983, at 8.66 feet above the baseline (currently defined as the average daily lowest-water level observed between 1983 and 2001). As of Saturday morning, the prediction for the maximum sea level this week was 8.8 feet, but by Sunday morning, the prediction was adjusted downward to 8.6 feet.

It's still possible that sea levels could exceed 9 feet. "That is all dependent on how much storm surge that we get," Navarrete said Saturday evening. "We can guarantee that we'll have at least a foot to a foot and a half due to thermal expansion because of our warmer waters," but it's the level of storm surge that comes with the storm that'll determine "if we are going to break records."

"Places that have rarely, or never, flooded before may be inundated," UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said. It's not rain falling from the sky that's the main threat; it's areas at risk of saltwater flooding from the ocean or the bay, he added.

The rain itself isn't expected to be as intense as last week's historic rainfall that hit the Bay Area, which brought 3.2 inches to San Francisco in two days. This week's storm could bring roughly 1.5 inches to San Francisco over two days — still substantial and impactful because it'll coincide with the king tides, Navarrete said.

The king tides — influenced solely by the position of the moon and sun — are large because we're near the peaks of what are known as the 18.6-year lunar node tidal cycle and the 4.4-year lunar perigee tidal cycle.

Record-breaking ocean temperatures are also influencing the high sea levels, since hotter water takes up more volume.

Southern California isn't getting a major storm this week. Still, meteorologists warned that areas spared from hurricanes Marie and Rachel in early September and early October, and from high tides Oct. 27, could get hit with coastal flooding this week.

In Orange and San Diego counties, forecasters with the National Weather Service warned of "extreme" risk from coastal flooding and high surf on Thanksgiving Day, and warned of "major" impacts from coastal flooding on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday.

Compared with the Oct. 27 coastal flooding — which damaged 114 homes and other structures in Huntington Beach alone, and also hit Newport Beach hard — this week's flooding may be worse, forecasters warned.

"It'll most likely be at least as bad as that, and it could be a little worse because we are actually expecting a little bit of higher surf," said Philip Gonsalves, meteorologist with the weather service office in San Diego, which also issues forecasts for Orange County.

With maximum sea level possibly exceeding 8 feet on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day, "this will bring widespread moderate-to-major coastal flooding," the weather service's San Diego office said. Newport Beach has been working to temporarily raise seawalls and build sand berms on beaches to prepare. Huntington Beach warned that low-lying roads will be closed Monday through Friday from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. daily, including a total closure of a 3.7-mile stretch of Pacific Coast Highway through the neighborhood of Sunset Beach — from Seal Beach Boulevard to Warner Avenue.

Huntington Beach also asked boaters to limit unnecessary travel through Huntington Harbour, since boat wakes — when tides are high — can "cause water to overtop seawalls and bulkheads, potentially flooding neighboring properties and damaging docks and private property."

In Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties, there's high confidence in record-breaking high tides, the weather service office in Oxnard said. The coastal flooding risk will be the highest on Wednesday and Thursday, exacerbated by elevated-to-high surf that peaks on those two days.

With a swell coming from the west, west-facing beaches are at high risk, including the L.A. County coast from Santa Monica to the Palos Verdes Peninsula and the Ventura County coast from Faria Beach to Silver Strand Beach, including the inside of the harbors and Ventura Pier, according to meteorologist Dave Gomberg of the weather service's Oxnard office.

The swell won't be as big in the Long Beach area, Gomberg said, but he's still concerned about the high maximum sea levels for the area. Crews have been adding sand to the shoreline of the Long Beach Peninsula, which was hit hard by swells from the south from hurricanes Marie and Rachel

Forecasters said Sunday there could be increased beach attendance due to very pleasant, warm air temperatures — in the 70s — in Southern California on Thanksgiving Day. However, more beachgoers, coupled with large waves, increases the likelihood of more beach rescues, and forecasters advised people planning beach visits to go to those with lifeguards.

On the Central Coast, areas of greatest concern include Morro Bay, Pismo Beach, Oceano Dunes, Cayuco Pier, Avila Beach Pier and Pismo Beach Pier.

Maximum sea level records could be broken yet again. On Oct. 27, the tide gauge in San Pedro broke a record, with a maximum sea level reaching 8.19 feet. A reasonable worst-case scenario for a maximum sea level on Wednesday in L.A. County would be up to 8.7 feet, the weather service said.

The flooding that came in late October occurred even though there wasn't significant surf. This time around, "we've got some larger surf," which can worsen coastal flooding, said meteorologist Lisa Phillips of the National Weather Service in Oxnard.

But there is some uncertainty. One factor that could result in lower-than-expected sea levels on Thanksgiving Day would be higher pressure moving over the area, which would "kind of squish the water down and may contribute to slightly lower levels of those tides," weather service meteorologist Bryan Lewis said.

Forecasters warned Sunday that the coastal threat could continue after this week. Another swell could threaten the Southern California coast starting again on the Sunday after Thanksgiving.

data.title: Jon Ossoff's decisive Senate win in Georgia fuels presidential buzz
data.description:
Politics

Ossoff's expanding coalition in Georgia fuels 2028 presidential buzz — even if he says he's not running

By
Fin Daniel Gómez
Political Director and Executive Director of Politics and White House, CBS News
Fin Daniel Gómez is CBS News' political director and executive director, Politics and White House. In this role, Gómez oversees the daily White House and political coverage for CBS News and works closely with Washington bureau leadership to inform the Network's political coverage.
Read Full Bio
Fin Daniel Gómez,
Zak Hudak,
Joe Walsh
Senior Editor, Politics
Joe Walsh is a senior editor for digital politics at CBS News. Joe previously covered breaking news for Forbes and local news in Boston.
Read Full Bio
Joe Walsh

November 22, 2026 / 4:06 PM EST / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding reelection victory in Georgia is drawing renewed attention to his potential as a 2028 presidential contender, as election data shows how he assembled a broad coalition of voters in the pivotal presidential battleground state.

Despite the growing speculation, Ossoff, 39, is for now dismissing the possibility of a White House bid. During a debate in October, Ossoff said he had "zero interest in running for president" in 2028.

Some early polls place him at the top of a hypothetical 2028 primary field. A post-election Emerson College survey showed Ossoff with the support of 17% of respondents — narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom rounding out the top five. 

Ossoff has attracted interest from both centrists and progressives while delivering a decisive victory in a closely divided presidential battleground state. At Crooked Con, a primarily progressive gathering in Washington after the midterms, Ossoff received 38% of first-choice votes in its straw poll, ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg.

"I think he would make an attractive presidential contender on the Democratic side," said Jerry Gonzalez, CEO of GALEO Impact Fund PAC, a Georgia-based Latino political action committee that endorsed Ossoff in his Senate race. "He is not afraid, he won't shy away from holding the Trump administration accountable, but in a way that works towards actually building coalitions to get something done." 

Democrats who can win statewide in conservative or swing states tend to be moderate, and that's true of Ossoff, too. 

"He comes across, and tries to present himself, as a moderate, and he talks about issues which moderate conservatives could get behind," said Charles Bullock, a longtime political science professor at the University of Georgia. "The issues he stresses are things which are within the broad mainstream of 'These would be good things.'"

It's unclear how well a moderate would fare in the early nominating states. What is effective in a Georgia general election may be a tougher sell in a Democratic primary, where voters often reward ideological purity over swing-state caution. 

"Obviously, he's successful here in Georgia," Bullock said. "How would he play elsewhere? 

"I think what we will be seeing is preparation, maybe for a later run," Bullock speculated. 

Ossoff's record gives rivals on both flanks openings to attack: progressives have criticized his vote for the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and his reluctance to embrace "Medicare for All," while his votes to restrict certain weapons sales to Israel and his criticism of its military conduct in Gaza have drawn objections from some pro-Israel Democrats and donors.

All of those issues are certain to be part of the 2028 primary contest. For example, Rep. Ro Khanna, another potential 2028 candidate, last week tried to restart the debate over universal healthcare. 

"Medicare for All means healthcare for everyone, like public school is free for every kid," Khanna wrote on X, arguing, "'Medicare for All who want it' is pablum. It's telling parents they have to pay for public school." 

In his reelection this month, Ossoff defeated GOP opponent Mike Collins by around 18 points, two years after President Trump defeated Harris by around two points in 2024. It was a much wider margin than his last Senate election, which he won by just over one percentage point.

Powering Ossoff's win this year was a broad coalition of voters, including some swing constituencies that Democrats have struggled with in recent years, CBS News' exit polling shows.

Ossoff maintained strong support among Black voters, winning 93% of the group, which make up almost one-third of the state's eligible voters according to Pew Research Center.

He did not win the White voters who make up just over half of Georgia's electorate, but he did make significant inroads, winning 40% — after Harris had won just 28% two years earlier. He also notched some improvement in groups that have shifted hard against Democrats: He won 29% of White voters without college degrees (compared to Harris' 18%) and 19% of White evangelical or born-again Christian voters (compared to less than 10% for Harris).

Ossoff also won men by nine points after Harris lost them by 13 points.

Both Ossoff and Harris won younger Georgians, but Ossoff won them by a larger margin, securing 85% of voters ages 29 and under. Ossoff also split the 45-and-older vote roughly in half, while Harris lost that age group by a 15-point margin.

And Ossoff made gains with Hispanics — a group that makes up less than 10% of Georgia's eligible voters but which has grown rapidly and has become a swing demographic that could decide a close race in the perennial battleground. In his reelection victory, he won around two-thirds of Latino voters, up seven points from Harris' performance two years earlier.

A comparison of 19 Georgia precincts where at least 30% of active registered voters identify as Hispanic or Latino shows substantial Democratic improvement.

Ossoff won those precincts by a combined 49 points in the two-candidate vote, compared with an eight-point advantage for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and an 18-point margin for fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022.

The changes were significant in areas that had supported Mr. Trump just two years earlier.

In six heavily Latino precincts in Whitfield County, the combined results shifted from a 12-point Trump advantage in 2024 to a 37-point Ossoff victory in 2026. Three similar precincts in Hall County shifted from an 11-point Trump edge to a 33-point Ossoff victory.

Those figures reflect the voting behavior of entire precincts rather than individual Latino voters, and comparisons between presidential and midterm electorates are not exact. Still, they underscore how dramatically the environment changed in places with large Latino populations.

Gonzalez attributed the shift in part to concerns over affordability and immigration enforcement, two issues he said weighed heavily on Latino voters in Georgia.

"Things are really expensive," Gonzalez told CBS News. "The price and affordability were a big driving issue." He also pointed to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and its impact on Latino communities in Georgia. Ossoff has investigated allegations of abuses in federal immigration detention facilities as part of his Senate oversight work.

Gonzalez also credited Ossoff's success among voters across the political spectrum to his accessibility and constituent outreach.

 "His office is accessible to all Georgians, and that's part of the reason why he won."

In this wave election, Ossoff wasn't the only Democrat to pick up ground in the midterms. Latino and Black voters, men, voters without college degrees and younger voters moved back toward Democratic candidates nationwide, a reversal after all four groups had shifted rightward in 2024.

In 2028, those groups could once again play a central role in both the Democratic Party's nominating process and the general election.

States with large Black and Latino populations will lead the Democratic primary calendar after the party rearranged its schedule, and Ossoff, with his strong support from both groups, would likely stand to benefit if he were to decide to run. South Carolina — where Black Democratic voters have long played an influential role in choosing the party's presidential nominee — will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

The DNC says approximately 4.2 million Latinos live across the six early nominating states, a major increase from the party's previous early-state lineup.

In the general election, maintaining a strong lead with Black, Latino and younger voters — and preventing too much slippage among White and non-college-educated voters — will also be a core task for Democrats, as they seek to prevent the GOP's first non-Trump presidential candidate in over a decade from reassembling the Trump coalition.

Though Ossoff says he doesn't plan a White House bid in 2028, his performance in Georgia has provided an early measure of what an electoral coalition for him could look like.

"He has mentioned that he was focused on winning reelection, which he has done, so I think that gives him a little bit of latitude to think about it a little more seriously," Gonzalez said.

data.title: ICE arrests by masked agents at Seattle airport enrage passengers and state officials
data.description:
'They're taking my dad': ICE arrests at Seattle airport enrage passengers, state officials

Brittny Mejia
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 7:51 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

'They're taking my dad': ICE arrests at Seattle airport enrage passengers, state officials

1 of 2

Screams rang out on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle, as two masked, plainclothes federal immigration officers detained a father and daughter as they boarded a flight bound for Los Angeles.

The daughter, identified by authorities as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, clung to an agent's leg as she pleaded: "Please, I beg you, I beg you, I beg you, no."

"They're taking my dad ... we have a work permit," she told fellow passengers. "I'm being arrested by ICE."

Advertisement

The Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, captured on multiple videos on Saturday morning and shared on social media, enraged state and local leaders, immigrant advocates and passengers who witnessed it. ICE has increased arrests at airports over the past year, including of foreign citizens with expired U.S. visas.

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson wrote on X. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight."

The Department of Homeland Security hit back at the governor, posting on X that officers had been targeting Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who overstayed his visa.

During the arrest, the agency said Hernandez "hurled hot coffee on the officers." The officers arrested Hernandez, who they said also overstayed her visa, and said she would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

In videos of the arrests, one officer appeared to have a stain on his jacket. A passenger seemingly contested that allegation, with one heard telling an officer: "She didn't throw coffee on you bro."

John Gaedeke, a passenger on the flight, told the Times that the plane was half loaded when he spotted the two men — who he later learned were officers — cutting the line. Gaedeke said he heard the men whisper to another, "Should we do it? There he is, let's go."

Soon after, Gaedeke said he saw the officers tackle a man and "then it just turned to chaos." People cried as they filmed, he said, and Alaska Airlines staff were "in a state of shock." A woman standing in front of him with her young son turned her body to protect him.

"She was obviously scared. Her son was petrified," Gaedeke said, describing what unfolded as "theatrical violence." "The instant grief from the family members, just the screaming, crying and wailing — that still sticks with me."

Gaedeke said it didn't look to him like the coffee was thrown at the agents. In his Instagram caption, he described the incident as "the most f— up thing I have personally witnessed in this country."

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said in a statement that immigration enforcement actions are conducted "without the Port's participation or knowledge." They said they were "outraged" by what occurred and were in conversation with Homeland Security on whether any protocols "were breached."

"This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred," the statement read.

Alaska Airlines said in a statement that they were "concerned" by what unfolded "during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306." The airline said it was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action "and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed."

"We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests," they said.

A GoFundMe launched for the father and daughter, which had raised more than $40,000 by Sunday morning, described the family as "very grateful for all the love and support that they have received so far from family, friends, and community leaders and members."

"Legal proceedings and the following events can be drawn out long-term and become very costly," Yareli Farias, who described herself as a close friend of the family, wrote on GoFundMe. "The funds raised will be used for legal expenses related to this case."

In a Saturday afternoon news conference, Katie Garrow, executive secretary-treasurer of MLK Labor, which represents thousands of unionized workers at the airport, said they were alerted to the arrests by flight attendants.

"They are the ones who rang the alarm that this escalation broke protocol and crossed a red line," Garrow said.

Garrow said the incident was "so disturbing and upsetting to workers" that four of the six crew members on Flight 1306 "chose not to fly" that morning.

At the news conference, Gov. Ferguson called video of the arrests "horrific" and "chilling." He described it as "the latest example of the violence that ICE has inflicted on our communities as it works to further Donald Trump's cruel immigration agenda."

"There is no justification for this brutality," Ferguson said.

Ferguson said he will request that every airline in the airport call on ICE "to get out of our airports."

"We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it," Ferguson said. "It is beyond reform ... It is time to abolish Donald Trump's ICE."

Times staff writer Matthew Ormseth contributed to this report.

data.title: Iranian attacks in Strait of Hormuz hit highest levels since war began
data.description:
A liquefied petroleum gas tanker burning in the Strait of Hormuz off the Musandam Peninsula, Oman, on Tuesday.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices.

In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the US-Iran war began in late February.

As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data. The reporting area covers the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.

Before October, the number of reported attacks in the region averaged around 10 per month. Numbers vary, but data from the International Maritime Organization also points to October as having the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year.

Since the conflict began, the strait has become a heavily contested frontier, with attacks there disrupting oil and gas shipping and sparking global economic fallout.

Iran began trying to halt traffic in the wake of the US-Israeli attacks that launched the war. In response, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and as CNN previously reported, Gulf producers have found ways of getting ships through the strait.

Commercial traffic through the channel – through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war – remains at a reduced level when compared to the 2025 baseline.

As global oil prices fall and the Iran’s domestic crude revenues come under increasing strain, Tehran has been stepping up attacks, with experts saying the country is losing its leverage over the waterway and could escalate attacks further in an attempt to force concessions from Washington.

No need for a deal, Trump says

The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports. Prices also fell after the US midterm results as concerns over fresh US military action in the Middle East subsided.

“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN. “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation.”

A man pumps fuel at a gas station in Miami, Florida, on November 10.

Meanwhile, Iran’s domestic oil revenues are falling sharply as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to stifle the country’s supply of oil to global markets, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler.

“Iranian oil on water outside the (US) blockade zone has hit zero as the last cargoes discharged in China earlier this month. Consequently, Iran’s oil revenues could drop to zero by mid-December,” Kpler reported in late October.

US President Donald Trump said this month the US doesn’t “need a deal” with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

He later indicated he wouldn’t hesitate to resume military strikes in Iran if necessary.

Three tankers struck in Hormuz since Friday

During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to Marisks, a maritime risk management company.

Marisks did not confirm who was behind the attacks, though it said Iranian involvement was “assessed as likely.”

Related vertical video

Trump says Iran is ‘bullsh*tting’ on effort to end war

Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow at 3 p.m. UTC (10 a.m. ET) on Friday. All crew were reported safe, Marisks said.

The Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged crude oil tanker, caught fire after being hit in the stern at 5 a.m. UTC on Saturday (midnight ET on Saturday). Less than an hour later, the Arina, also Hong Kong-flagged, was struck in the engine room by a missile.

The attacks demonstrate the “continued critical threat” to commercial shipping in the region, Marisks said, particularly through the “southern corridor” near Oman’s coastline which Iran vehemently opposes.

CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Laura Sharman, Nadeen Ebrahim and Alayna Treene contributed reporting.

data.title: Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats — the largest since 1992
data.description:
Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992

JILL COLVIN and LISA MASCARO
Updated Sun, November 22, 2026 at 6:07 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Congress

1 of 6
The U.S. Capitol is seen, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Advertisement

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."

Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change."

Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."

A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority — meaning any few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's highwater marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

Sun, November 22, 2026 at 3:41 PM UTC
2 min read

By Katharine Jackson and Ross Kerber

WASHINGTON/BOSTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that it would be difficult ‌for him to work with Senator Chuck Schumer if the ‌Democrat is elected Senate majority leader.

"It is going to be very hard for me ​to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst [in] history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again."

Advertisement

Schumer, a ‌New York Democrat, is currently ⁠minority leader in the Senate but Democrats next year will take control of both chambers of Congress after ⁠sweeping wins in midterm elections earlier this month.

Despite the midterm wins, Schumer faces dissatisfied progressives who say a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers needs new leadership.

Maryland ​Senator Chris ​Van Hollen is making a bid for ​the Senate leadership, although Schumer has said ‌he has the votes to continue as leader. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for next month.

After the elections, Trump appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller to run the White House, suggesting the president will take an even more confrontational approach in his last two years in office. But ‌Trump also has hinted he might work ​with Democrats on issues such as healthcare.

Speaking ​on CNN on Sunday, Senator-elect ​Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, said she supported expanding ‌Medicare to cover all Americans. "If we ​have to call ​it TrumpCare in order to get it across the finish line, that's fine by me," she said.

Flanagan said she would support Van ​Hollen for majority ‌leader. "What we heard from voters is that they were pushing back ​against the status quo," Flanagan said.

data.title: World's longest climate summit ends without a deal after fossil fuel dispute
data.description:
1. Climate
  2. News

Cop31 ends with no deal as longest climate summit ever collapses into disarray

Countries fail to reach agreement on text, which omitted mentions of fossil fuels, after hours of negotiations in Turkey

Stuti Mishra & Nicole Wootton-Cane
Sunday 22 November 2026 15:56 GMT
  • Bookmark
  • Comments
    Go to comments

Bookmark popover

Removed from bookmarks

Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Join today

Already a member? Log in

The Cop31 climate summit in Turkey descended into disarray and disappointment after countries were unable to reach consensus on a deal that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Nations rejected the agreement at a fraught closing session in Antalya on Sunday, almost two days after the summit was due to finish in what stretched to become the longest Cop in history.

The European Union, the UK and small island states such as Tuvalu refused to accept the text over the absence of fossil fuels, blasting the omissions as “greenwashing” and accusing oil states of “hijacking” the talks.

Ireland’s minister for climate Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, called the text “unconscionable” and said its ambition went “nowhere near the level of action that's required to deal with climate change”. A spokesperson for the British delegation said it was “profoundly disappointed” by the proposed deal.

Some nations indicated a willingness to continue working, but at the closing plenary summit president ⁠Murat ​Kurum said ⁠there would be no new ⁠draft of the ​deal.

Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to attend the summit, where he made an impassioned speech promising to usher in a “new era of British leadership" on climate change.

But the prime minister said nothing on Sunday as hopes of a deal evaporated and delegates eventually left empty handed.

UK energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh later called the failure to reach a deal “immensely disappointing” but said there had been “genuine progress” during the conference.

“This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it,” she said in a statement. “The moment required bold ambition and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”

The failed deal had acknowledged the planet's projected temperature overshoot for the first time and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.

It was already heavily criticised by small islands and civil society groups who called it a “betrayal” and criticised its reliance on carbon capture schemes, which had been pushed by oil states including Saudi Arabia.

"It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis," Maina Talia, Tuvalu's climate minister, commented during the conference.

A representative for the Saudi delegation, which supported the deal's mention of carbon removal, told the summit he was surprised at the ‌resistance to technology, which he said offered a “concrete solution”.

Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new funds to ​help them adapt to a warming planet.

China and India said they had objections but chose to accept the cover text to move things forward.

Earlier, Mr Kurum, defended the text and said the presidencies had “listened to everyone” and tried to bring the groups together, but admitted there was “no consensus”.

Australia's Cop31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome "very disappointing" and said disagreements over fuels ​and ⁠climate finance were the dealbreakers.

The conference became the longest COP ever on Sunday afternoon, passing COP25 in Madrid in 2019, which ran 44 hours over its schedule.

Delegates pored over several drafts with language that tried to bridge the position of countries most exposed to climate impacts and those whose economies depend on producing or consuming fossil fuels, but the split came down to whether the text should refer to oil, gas and coal at all.

The first time the transition away from fossil fuels found a mention in a UN climate agreement was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023. It had been hoped that a series of climate disasters in the lead up to this year’s conference would help to sharpen minds and reaffirm commitments.

The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

Chief executive of environmental charity Friends of the Earth Asad Rehman said the deal in its current form “is no deal at all” and urged governments to pledge more than “wooly” promises.

He warned leaders the “clock is ticking” and said governments must “come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver”.

United Nationals general secretary Antonio Guterres also said he was "deeply disappointed” by the conference’s failure to reach a consensus.

“I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” he said. "There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."

Some campaigners also turned on the EU, which rejected the text while some lauded the resistance shown at the plenary.

"The EU is trying to shift blame onto others and it is deeply hypocritical. At the beginning of COP31, it signalled it was prepared to drop the renewables ask from the electrification target and it has failed to put forward an EU fossil fuel transition roadmap," said Laurie van der Burg of Oil Change International.

The failure is a blow to efforts to ratchet up international ‌action, but does not erase the obligations agreed by previous ‌summits or remove existing agreements on action against climate change.

data.title: Schumer's big Senate victory hasn't silenced Democrats who want him replaced
data.description:
Schumer led Democrats to big Senate win. Now, some say they need a new leader

By Nolan D. McCaskill
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:05 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Nolan D. McCaskill

WASHINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Chuck Schumer led Senate Democrats through November's midterm elections that gave them a decisive 56-seat majority. Progressives responded with a collective "thank you, next," arguing he should now make way for a successor.

Critics say Schumer's decades in Washington, his age and his close ties to the ‌party establishment make him ill-suited to lead a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.

Advertisement

"We write first to thank you," leaders of the populist Working Families Party, ‌which backs like-minded Democratic candidates in elections, said in a November 13 letter to Schumer that called for a generational leadership change.

"If you step aside at the height of a victory you helped secure, you would show voters ​that the Democratic Party heeded their call for change. The new majority can begin its work united and focused on fighting for the people who elected them."

The top Democrat in the Senate for the past decade, Schumer, who turns 76 on Monday, has projected confidence that his colleagues will choose to keep him as their leader in a secret vote on December 1.

"I will be elected majority leader," Schumer, who is strongly favored to win, told reporters matter-of-factly last week.

But in the first contested Senate Democratic leadership race since 1994, the New York senator faces a challenge from ‌Senator Chris Van Hollen, 67. While only modestly younger than Schumer, ⁠the Maryland lawmaker and his progressive allies outside the Capitol have cast him as an agent of change.

Van Hollen has said the 2026 results show voters are demanding the party break with the status quo and adopt a bolder approach that gives new voices, including incoming progressive lawmakers, more ⁠influence in the caucus.

'TIME FOR NEW IDEAS'

The Maryland Democrat has run an increasingly public campaign, though the outcome will be determined in private by 56 Senate Democrats. At least 16 Democrats have publicly committed to backing Schumer, while only six have said they will vote for Van Hollen.

"I'm in this to win it," Van Hollen said on Thursday. "That's my goal. I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious ​agenda ​like this, we need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic caucus. People need ​to have more input. Our new members need to be at ‌the table."

Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in November, including in several states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of the incoming freshmen said during their campaigns that they would oppose Schumer for Democratic leader.

"Do I like Chuck Schumer?" asked Senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine. "He's been great, but I do think it's time for new ideas."

In an interview last week on CNN's "State of the Union," Van Hollen cited a "hunger for change" among Senate Democrats and said two incoming senators won despite Schumer's efforts to back their primary opponents. He criticized Schumer for aligning with powerful pro-Israel and cryptocurrency interests in those races.

PROGRESSIVES BACK VAN HOLLEN

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said Van Hollen stands out because he understands how Washington and the Senate work as a past ‌chair of House and Senate Democrats' respective campaign arms, and he's willing to take risks.

"Those two things ​are what we need right now, and we need to rethink the way we legislate," he said, pointing to ​Van Hollen's trips to advocate for a wrongly deported migrant and to draw ​attention to Israel's war in Gaza as examples of his willingness to take risks.

Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia suggested the leadership fight reflected a healthy ‌discussion within the caucus about its future direction. "And there's nothing wrong with ​that," he told Reuters.

Senate Democratic leader is the ​only unresolved role among Congress' top four positions. House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress, where John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

SCHUMER COULD FACE PRIMARY CHALLENGER IN 2028

Schumer is up for reelection in 2028, ​and losing the leadership race could make him a more vulnerable ‌target, as ambitious Democrats such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez consider running for his seat. A memo from Ocasio-Cortez's campaign acknowledged she could run for president, Senate or reelection to ​the House in 2028.

For his part, Schumer has swatted down questions about his future beyond the leadership election.

"I'm focused on 2027 and delivering for the American ​people," he said on Wednesday.

(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: Washington governor calls for ICE to be abolished after arrests at Seattle airport
data.description:
‘ICE is completely and totally out of control’: Gov. Ferguson speaks out against Sea-Tac ICE arrest

Heather Bosch
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 8:01 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

On the eve of one of the busiest holiday travel weeks of the year, ICE agents arrested two people at SeaTac Airport Saturday.

The arrests, captured in a now viral video, are raising eyebrows and concerns.

In the video, provided to KIRO 7 by iceout.org, masked men can be see surrounding a man and woman on the floor of the jet bridge, where passengers had walked down to board Alaska Flight 1306 to Los Angeles.

Advertisement

As the chaotic scene unfolds, passengers can be heard asking the agents to identify themselves. They don't appear to do so. The woman on the ground says her name is Sophia, shouting "We have a work permit!"

The Port of Seattle said the agents took the two down to the tarmac, where they were put in a car and driven away.

In a post on X, US Customs and Immigration Enforcement confirmed it arrested Sophia Hernandez Mejioa and Ricardo Larrando Mendoza, because they overstayed their visas from Mexico. They added Hernandez Mejioa will be charged with assaulting a federal officer, for allegedly throwing a cup of coffee at one.

"Look, ICE is completely and totally out of control. And today, we are confronted with yet more evidence of this," Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said at a news conference. "The culture of ICE is bankrupt. It lacks morals. It lacks any decency. It is un-American. It is deeply, deeply un- American. And it must be abolished and replaced with something that is more sane."

Gov. Ferguson called on airlines to demand that ICE be barred from airports. In a statement, Alaska Airlines indicated it was not told about the ICE enforcement action ahead of time.

Both the Governor and Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed, who was also at the news conference, said they'd been working to determine if the ICE agents broke any laws.

"The reality is that federal agents do have access throughout the airport, using their federal badges," Mohamed added. "That does give them access that is very different from even employees at the airport."

She confirmed to KIRO 7's Heather Bosch that the Port is not warned ahead of time about ICE enforcement at the airport, though Mohamed says she has requested that.
